result.title: ICEF Sustainable Data Centers Roadmap - Chapter 2.4: Heat Reuse
result.summary: Chapter from the ICEF Sustainable Data Centers Roadmap analyzing data-center waste-heat recovery opportunities. Covers challenges of heat reuse from air-cooled vs. liquid-cooled systems, evaluates reuse pathways (district heating, direct air capture, ORC electricity generation, aquaculture/agriculture), documents 12 operating and 13 planned projects globally, and recommends adoption of high-temperature liquid-cooling systems (45–70°C exit) and government mandates (10–20% heat reuse for new data centers, exemplified by Germany's requirement). Emphasizes that liquid-cooling systems enable heat recovery not feasible with traditional air-cooling.

key_articles.requirement: Data center operators should adopt high-temperature liquid-cooling systems (direct-chip or immersion cooling) that achieve exit temperatures of 45–70 °C for effective heat reuse in applications such as district heating

National and subnational governments should require feasibility studies for heat reuse in permitting large new datacenter projects and offer incentives; should consider requiring 10–20% heat reuse mandates for new data centers (such as in Germany)

District heating utilities and municipal planners should proactively partner with datacenter developers to map potential synergies and create or extend thermal infrastructure connecting data centers to buildings, industrial users and aquaculture facilities

result.temperature_signals: High-grade waste heat (45–70 °C) from modern liquid-cooled data centers aligns well with district heating system design in Nordic and EU countries, which typically operate at 60–70 °C input and 50 °C return. This temperature band eliminates the need for intermediate heating and enables direct thermal integration. In contrast, air-cooled data centers produce exit temperatures close to ambient (typically 20–25 °C), making heat recovery economically infeasible. Low-temperature heat (45–70 °C) is also suitable for industrial processes, aquaculture, and greenhouses. Direct air capture applications require 90–120 °C, necessitating heat pumps and additional electrical input, reducing the net energy benefit of data-center heat reuse. ORC (Organic Rankine Cycle) systems tested at 58 °C (representative of DC liquid-cooled output) demonstrated stability problems in temperate-zone climates with summer ambient temperatures exceeding 35 °C, making them unsuitable as sole cooling solutions. The document emphasizes that liquid-cooled data centers with ultra-high rack densities (>100 kW/cabinet) and immersion cooling achieve exit temperatures of 55–70 °C, capturing >99% of waste heat at grades suitable for immediate district heating use.
result.transaction_cost_signals: Heat reuse projects face significant administrative and infrastructural costs: (1) Proximity matching: high capital cost for underground pipes, pumping stations, and control systems to connect data centers to distant heat hosts; (2) Regulatory compliance: feasibility studies required for large new data center permits in jurisdictions with heat reuse policies (e.g., Germany), adding planning burden; (3) Interagency coordination: alignment required between data center operators, district heating utilities, and municipal planners on technologies, schedules, and business models—complex negotiations can delay or block projects; (4) Seasonal infrastructure: in regions with seasonal heating demand, data centers must invest in alternative summer heat rejection (cooling towers), doubling cooling infrastructure capital costs; (5) Technology certification and standards: lack of mature guidelines and matchmaking tools for heat host identification (though OCP and URBANopt platforms are being developed); (6) Government incentive uncertainty: most jurisdictions rarely offer subsidies, forcing operators to bear full project costs unless mandated by regulation (Germany example shows mandate increases feasibility but requires compliance monitoring). These barriers explain why only 12 operating and 13 planned projects >5 MW capacity exist globally despite clear technical feasibility at higher temperatures.
notable_quotes: "Liquid Cooling systems can enable reuse of heat that would otherwise be wasted. These systems have exit temperatures as high as 70 °C, limited only by the safe operating range of the chips. In liquid cooling systems, heat can be recycled at 45-70 °C, aligning with the thermal cycles in many district heating systems." (Section B: Opportunities)

"District heating systems in Nordic countries use moderate-temperature water--typically input at 60-70 °C and returned in the vicinity of 50 °C. These are excellent matches to modern liquid-cooling systems, but in order to optimize district heating, data centers need to be carefully planned to integrate with district heating options." (Section B.i: District heating)

"Data center operators should adopt high-temperature liquid-cooling systems--such as direct-chip or immersion cooling--that achieve exit temperatures of 45-70 °C, enabling effective heat reuse in applications, such as district heating." (Recommendation 1)
"National and subnational governments should consider requiring 10-20% heat reuse mandates for new data centers (such as in Germany)." (Recommendation 2)

result.title: Profitable Heat Recovery with Open District Heating - Annex 47 Case Study
result.summary: This is a case study documenting the Bahnhof Pionen data center's waste heat recovery project in Stockholm, Sweden, operated by Stockholm Energi under an "Open District Heating" business model. result.title: ANSI/ASHRAE Addendum g to ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 90.4-2022: Energy Standard for Data Centers
result.summary: ASHRAE 90.4-2022 Addendum g is a technical standard for data center energy efficiency approved by ANSI on January 31, 2024. It establishes design requirements and compliance metrics for data center HVAC systems, including the Annualized Mechanical Load Component (MLC) and Energy Loss Component (ELC) as key efficiency metrics. The standard modifies Sections 3, 4, and 6 to regulate process heat and ventilation, with specific design value thresholds for mechanical equipment serving data centers across multiple climate zones.

key_articles.topic: Scope and Applicability - New and Existing Buildings
key_articles.requirement: Mechanical equipment and systems installed to serve the heating, cooling, and ventilating needs of data center spaces in new buildings shall comply with requirements of Section 4.2.1.1. New mechanical equipment in additions to existing buildings shall comply with Section 4.1.2 as described in Section 11. Where existing HVAC air is provided to data center space in an addition by using existing HVAC systems and equipment, such existing systems need not be required to comply with this standard. However, any new systems or equipment installed must comply with specific requirements applicable to those systems and equipment. Where existing HVAC systems and equipment are extended to a data center addition, such existing systems and equipment shall not be required to comply with this standard.

key_articles.topic: Maximum Annualized Mechanical Load Component (MLC) and Design Value Thresholds
key_articles.requirement: Annualized MLC shall be calculated using Equation 6.5 and the resulting value shall be less than or equal to the value in Table 6.5 'Maximum Annualized Mechanical Load Component (Maximum Annualized MLC)'. The equation incorporates MechE values at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% ITE design, divided by the quantity (2.5 × 8760 hours × ITE design power). Compliance requires separate calculation for 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% ITE capacity.

For a facility being renovated where only one or two of the annualized MLC segments is being modified, compliance requirements in Table 6.5 apply only to the segments being modified. Trade-offs are allowed among process cooling, process heating, and process ventilation segment values to meet the aggregate requirement of only those annualized MLC segments involved in the project's scope.

key_articles.topic: MLC Calculation Compliance Requirements and Operating Units (N)
key_articles.requirement: Annual energy calculations shall be completed separately for 100% and for part-load ITE capacity. Weather data shall be based on one of the following: NSRB Typical Meteorological Year Version (TMY3) for a site with location and altitude nearest the data center site. Weather data shall be divided into calculation bins with a maximum 2°F (1°C) increment. Systems using an evaporative process will use wet-bulb temperature for creating binsihins; systems with non-evaporative process shall use dry-bulk temperature with mean coincident wet-bulb moisture ratio. Full hourly calculations (using 8760 bins, each of one hour) are also acceptable to use.

key_articles.topic: Cooling Energy, Heating Energy, and Process Ventilation Segments
key_articles.requirement: Cooling energy shall include input energy from chillers, heat pumps, air conditioners, fan systems part of any cooling or heat rejection system, pump systems part of any cooling or heat rejection system, relief fans required due to seasonal direct use of outdoor air, and cooling towers and other heat rejection systems. Cooling energy shall not include fans intrinsic to the ITE, fans intrinsic to UPS equipment, or cooling energy required for ventilation or makeup air if already included in the process ventilation segment. Heating energy shall include input energy from heaters associated with generators, heaters for freeze protection, and other heating sources. Heating energy shall not include input energy from heat recovery systems or heating energy for ventilation or makeup air already included in the process ventilation segment.

Construction documents shall require that, within 90 days after the date of system acceptance, record drawings of the actual installation be provided to the building owner or designated representative of the building owner. Record drawings shall include, as a minimum, the location and performance data on each piece of equipment, general configuration of the duct and pipe distribution system, including sizes, the terminal air (in units per calculation) to be installed and locations for all deferred equipment. Describe amounts of mechanical and electrical equipment assumed (in each part-load MLC compliance calculation) to be installed and operating during the 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% ITE power level in the associated MLC compliance calculation.

An alternative compliance method is provided in Section 11 that allows calculation of design professional's annualized MLC by modeling the routine intended electrical and mechanical efficiency for each hour, or an at a standard local year's weather across several ITE part-load power levels. The resulting calculated value, once reviewed, becomes the annualized MLC compliance value for that particular electrical and mechanical design for that data center's initial construction or subsequent modification.

result.temperature_signals: The standard defines baseline design temperatures for cooling calculations: HVAC ΔT (return air temperature) of 20°F (11°C) and exhaust air temperature of 85°F (29°C) establish the design conditions for process cooling segment values. Process heating segment values for data center ITE design power exceeding 300 kW are based on an indoor heated space meeting ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1 insulation requirements. For process ventilation, systems with thermal envelope compliance can operate with design temperatures constrained to maximum 460 hours annually outside Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments (4th Edition). The process ventilation segment compliance value is based only on minimum ambient air flow (3.8 cfm per kW), allowing economizer designs and temperature-varying outdoor air exchange per process cooling or process ventilation reduction with economizer designs. Temperature-based design points affect which climate zone thresholds apply for Annualized MLC (zones 0A through 8, with progressively stricter thresholds as climate becomes cooler/more favorable for free cooling).
result.transaction_cost_signals: Administrative burdens include: (1) Annualized MLC calculations required for 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% ITE capacity separately, using weather data divided into bins with maximum 2°F (1°C) increments or 8760 hourly bins, invoking multiple meteorological datasets and simulation tools; (2) Record drawings must be submitted within 90 days of system acceptance, documenting location, performance data, configuration details, and equipment assumptions at four power load levels—requiring coordination between contractors, design professionals, and building owners; (3) For partial renovations, trade-off analysis required between process cooling, heating, and ventilation segments to demonstrate aggregate compliance; (4) Alternative compliance method (Section 11) requires design professional modeling of routine electrical and mechanical efficiency across multiple ITE part-load levels and standard-year weather, with reviewer sign-off before value becomes compliance benchmark; (5) Compliance verification tied to specific design conditions (HVAC ΔT, exhaust temperature, outdoor air minimums) necessitating detailed HVAC specification and review. The standard permits flexibility in trade-offs and alternative pathways but requires rigorous documentation and third-party review, creating significant transaction costs for design documentation, submission, and verification workflows.
notable_quotes: Addendum g modifies Sections 3 and 6 to support the regulation of process heat and process ventilation. Specific details about any heated standby generators or ventilation or humidity control equipment systems new will be necessary to include in the MLC. (Foreword, page 3)

annualized mechanical load component (annualized MLC): the sum of all cooling, fan, pump and heat rejection annual energy use divided by the data center ITE energy the result of dividing the sum of the annual process cooling energy, annual process heating energy, and annual process ventilation energy by the annual total data center energy as precisely defined by Equation 6.5. (Section 3 Definition)

The baseline process cooling MLC values provided in Table 6.5 were based on simulation data for a mechanical system designed to condition only the ITE equipment. The energy simulations did not include cooling for UPS and other electrical losses. To accommodate these increases in annual energy for data center HVAC, the project maximum MLC mechanical compliance target values in Table 6.5 were made less stringent (larger). (Foreword, page 3)

For data center designs where heat recovery measures are being provided, Equation 6.5 shall be calculated for compliance with each of the design's heat recovery measures either 'active' or 'inactive' (at the discretion of the design professional.). Informative Note: This standard leaves all energy or emission savings credits available for the benefit of the data center's host or neighboring projects, without the possibility of double counting such energy or emission credits. (Section 6.5.2, page 5-6)

result.title: ASHRAE TC9.9 Data Center Power Equipment Thermal Guidelines and Best Practices
result.summary: ASHRAE TC9.9 whitepaper (2016) establishes thermal guidelines and design recommendations for data center power equipment operating in IT environments. It specifies thermal classes (A1-A4, B, C) with recommended and allowable inlet temperature/humidity ranges, defines temperature rise limits, and provides guidance for power equipment to coexist with IT equipment in shared physical spaces. Key implication for waste-heat recovery: higher allowable inlet temperatures (up to 45°C for Class A4) enable capture of warmer exhaust air as a heat source, directly supporting low-to-medium-grade waste heat recovery applications.

key_articles.requirement: Six thermal classes defined with specific dry-bulb temperature ranges, humidity limits, dew point, maximum elevation, and temperature change rates. Recommended range for all classes: 18-27°C (A1-A4) dry-bulb, -9°C to 15°C dew point. Class A3 and A4 allowable ranges extend to 40-45°C respectively.

key_articles.ref: Section 2.1 - ASHRAE Thermal Guideline Classes for IT Equipment Spaces
key_articles.requirement: Original 2004 ASHRAE guidelines recommended 20-25°C (68-77°F). Classes A3 (40°C / 104°F) and A4 (45°C / 113°F) were created in 2011 to support economization and energy savings technologies while maintaining equipment reliability.
Design power equipment to meet IEC61439 requirements at minimum 40°C (104°F) per ASHRAE Class A3; prefer 40°C as design point. Applies to equipment in ballroom, cold aisle, and grey areas.

key_articles.topic: Rack PDU Maximum Ambient Temperature Rating
key_articles.requirement: Design rack PDUs for maximum ambient air temperature rating of at least 60°C (140°F) to align with rising IT equipment exhaust temperatures in hot aisles. Above 60°C may be needed if exhaust temperatures continue rising.

Locate power equipment in ballroom, cold aisle, or grey areas where possible to minimize temperature de-rating. Avoid hot aisles. Ballroom and cold aisle temperatures typically do not require de-rating; hot aisle temperatures necessitate de-rating.

key_articles.ref: Section 3 - Temperature Ratings for Power Equipment
key_articles.requirement: Power equipment de-rates based on conductor temperature rise: Maximum Tc = ΔTc + Ta, where Tc is conductor temperature rating, Ta is ambient air temperature, ΔTc is temperature rise under power loading. Allows flexible capacity over wide temperature range if de-rated per manufacturer guidelines.

key_articles.ref: Section 2.3 - Rising Exhaust Temperature of IT Equipment
key_articles.requirement: IT equipment exhaust temperatures increased approximately 10°C (18°F) over 8 years (2008-2020). At 35°C inlet, exhaust can reach 45-58°C; at 45°C inlet, servers reach 58-60°C (140°F). Figure 6-8 document server temperature rise projections.
Metal surfaces: 60°C brief contact, 55°C longer duration; Plastic/Rubber: 85°C brief, 75°C longer duration. Power equipment must comply with touch temperature limits.

key_articles.ref: Section 4 - Medium and Low Voltage Switchgear (IEC 61439)
key_articles.requirement: Per IEC 61439, ambient temperature specification for low/medium voltage switchgear is maximum 35°C (95°F) with 2-hour excursion allowed to 40°C (104°F). Hygrostat and panel heaters control humidity to prevent condensation.

Most VRLA batteries may not be suitable for IT equipment spaces economizing over temperature range wider than 18 to 27°C (64-81°F). Lead-acid battery lifetime highly temperature-dependent; ideal temperature 25°C (77°F); operating above this shortens lifespan.

compliance_triggers.condition: Power equipment shares physical space and air stream with IT equipment

compliance_triggers.consequence: VRLA batteries may not be suitable for UPS systems in those spaces; alternative battery technology or dedicated temperature-controlled zones required

compliance_triggers.condition: Power equipment located in hot aisle or exhaust path of IT equipment
compliance_triggers.consequence: Ambient temperature will exceed cold-aisle design point; de-rating of power capacity may be necessary, or higher-temperature-rated equipment must be specified per manufacturer de-rating formula

compliance_triggers.condition: External surfaces of power equipment (e.g., bus bars, panel faces) approach or exceed touch temperature limits
compliance_triggers.consequence: Equipment design must use panel heaters, insulation, or alternative materials (plastic vs. metal) to stay below IEC60950-1 touch limits (60°C metal brief, 55°C longer; 85°C plastic brief, 75°C longer)

compliance_triggers.condition: Power equipment with super-capacitors is installed in variable-temperature IT space
compliance_triggers.consequence: De-rating calculations must use component manufacturer temperature/voltage de-rating guidelines; temperature and humidity monitoring during shipping/storage required; must comply with equipment specification limits (typically max non-operational 45°C/113°F)

compliance_triggers.condition: Data center implements aisle containment strategy with hot-aisle recirculation
compliance_triggers.consequence: Power equipment in same row as IT equipment must draw cooling air from cold aisle and exhaust to hot aisle in similar configuration to IT equipment to support aisle containment efficiency

compliance_triggers.condition: Data center operates economization such that outdoor/cooled air is used for IT inlet, but switchgear is in non-economized ballroom or separate area
compliance_triggers.consequence: Switchgear ambient temperature specification per IEC 61439 (35°C max, 40°C excursion max 2 hours) may constrain IT space economization range if equipment is proximate

compliance_triggers.condition: Power distribution equipment (line cords, receptacles, terminals) is located in raised floor plenum or under hot aisle
compliance_triggers.consequence: Cord ampacity must be calculated to allow full current-carrying capability over ambient temperature range around cord (recommended design point 60°C); de-rating tables must account for actual ambient in that location

compliance_triggers.condition: Data center plans to harvest IT equipment exhaust for district heating or waste-heat recovery process
compliance_triggers.consequence: Power equipment in hot aisle must be rated to tolerate exhaust temperatures (58-60°C at 45°C inlet, 45-58°C at 35°C inlet); design specifications must align with waste-heat grade (low/medium); maximum ambient rating of ≥60°C required for Rack PDU
compliance_triggers.applies_to: Both DC operator and heat off-taker

result.temperature_signals: This document is core to understanding temperature-grade classification for DC waste-heat recovery. Key signals: (1) ASHRAE Class A3 (5-40°C allowable range) and A4 (5-45°C) enable higher inlet temperatures, directly increasing exhaust temperature to 45-60°C—a LOW-to-MEDIUM-grade heat band suitable for district heating integration. (2) Power equipment must be "de-rated" when exposed to higher ambient; this de-rating penalty (reduced power capacity) incentivizes moving power equipment OUT of hot aisles into cold aisles or ballrooms, where cooler inlet (18-27°C typical) preserves full capacity. (3) Exhaust temperature trend: IT equipment is trending hotter (ΔT increased ~10°C over 8 years), meaning at Class A4 inlet (45°C), exhaust now reaches 58-60°C—at the threshold of medium-grade heat (MedT manufacturing tier ~50-70°C). (4) Touch temperature and equipment durability constraints limit how far power equipment ratings can climb; rack PDUs rated only to 60°C ambient suggest practical ceiling for long-term reliability of power gear colocated with IT in hot spaces. (5) Switchgear locked to IEC 61439 (35°C baseline, 40°C excursion)—incompatible with Class A4 economization; must be relocated to separate, cooled zones, adding spatial/piping cost for WHR schemes. IMPLICATION: Waste-heat recovery at DC scale is feasible for LowT (25-45°C, typical cold-aisle + mild economization) and MedT (45-70°C, aggressive hot-aisle + high-T power gear), but requires deliberate thermal zoning and power equipment placement strategy.
result.transaction_cost_signals: ASHRAE TC9.9 identifies multiple transaction costs for aligning power and IT equipment in warmer, economized data centers: (1) De-rating analysis: power equipment manufacturers must publish de-rating curves or multipliers for wide temperature ranges (especially Class A3/A4); DC operators must calculate reduced capacity and verify compliance—adds engineering burden and may require oversized equipment to maintain full output. (2) Equipment specification expansion: older equipment designed to 2004 guidelines (20-25°C) cannot operate reliably at 40-45°C without upgrade; mixed-vintage equipment compatibility requires case-by-case thermal certification. (3) Touch temperature and material substitution: external surfaces must respect IEC60950-1 limits; panel heaters, insulation, or plastic substitution for metal adds design and cost complexity. (4) Battery and capacitor management: super-capacitor de-rating, VRLA unsuitability in wide-temperature spaces, and temperature/humidity monitoring requirements add capital and operational overhead. (5) Switchgear relocation: IEC 61439 constraint (35°C max) forces medium/low-voltage switchgear OUT of hot-aisle environments; requires separate cooled zones, additional HVAC, piping, and infrastructure investment that DC operator must bear. (6) Hot-aisle equipment rating escalation: Rack PDU minimum of 60°C (recommended by ASHRAE) demands higher-specification equipment than traditional cool-aisle designs, increasing procurement cost. (7) Metering and monitoring: ASHRAE Rec. 15 mandates real-time air temperature monitoring at multiple locations to prevent thermal excursions and de-rating penalties; adds instrumentation and control system cost. (8) Cord and cable amphacity re-calculation: extended ambient ranges require detailed ampacity derating per NEC/IEC; engineering review mandatory for compliance. (9) Warranty and reliability risk: operating power equipment at elevated temperatures (40-45°C sustained) reduces component lifespan and warranty coverage; DC operators face higher replacement frequency and supply-chain risk. OVERALL: Regulatory alignment of power/IT equipment for economization and WHR imposes significant upfront engineering, capital (equipment + infrastructure), and ongoing monitoring/optimization costs on DC operators—a major friction point for WHR viability.
notable_quotes: Design power equipment to meet the temperature and humidity requirements of IEC61439 at a minimum and preferably to the 40°C (104°F) temperature requirement of ASHRAE Class A3. 40°C (104°F) is already a de-facto industry standard design point for most power equipment. This recommendation applies to power equipment residing in the ballroom, cold aisle, and grey areas of the data center. (Recommendation 1, Section 8)

Design rack PDUs for a maximum ambient air temperature rating of at least 60°C (140°F). This is needed to align with rising IT equipment exhaust temperatures in the hot aisle. If IT equipment exhaust temperatures continue to increase in the future, ratings above 60°C (140°F) may be needed. (Recommendation 3, Section 8)

Exhaust temperature rise for air inlet temperatures of 35°C (95°F) and 45°C (113°F) are shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8. At the inlet air temperature rises to 35°C (95°F), most servers reach a maximum exhaust air temperature somewhere between 58 and 60°C (140°F). For power distribution infrastructure (i.e. line cords, facility receptacles, etc.) located in a hot aisle or exhaust path of IT equipment there may be operating limitations due to 1) maximum rated temperature of a component, which may be addressed by using de-rating, or 2) maximum ambient temperature as referenced in some IEC standards. (Section 2.3, page 13)

Most VRLA batteries may not be suitable for IT equipment spaces where the data center is economizing over a temperature range wider than 18 to 27°C (64°F to 81°F). The lifetime of most lead-acid based VRLA batteries is very temperature dependent and operating these batteries at temperatures much above the ideal temperature of 25°C (77°F) may not practical or cost effective. (Recommendation 13, Section 8)

result.title: Comprehensive Assessment 2024 - Denmark (Bilag 13)
result.summary: Denmark's 2024 comprehensive assessment under EED Article 25 evaluates economically viable heat recovery potential from waste heat and high-efficiency combined heat and power production across all sectors. The document includes methodological frameworks for cost-benefit analysis, scenarios for heating/cooling system development through 2050, and assessment of surplus waste heat resources. Data centres are not explicitly addressed as a primary focus, but the assessment covers general industrial waste heat recovery economics and infrastructure.

key_articles.requirement: Member States shall conduct comprehensive assessments of their economically viable potential for high-efficiency cogeneration and heating and cooling production from renewable sources and waste heat recovery
Assessment must cover heating and cooling demand, supply options, economically viable potential, and barriers to high-efficiency systems

key_articles.topic: Effective District Heating and Cooling Definition
key_articles.requirement: Implemented per EED Article 26.1, with focus on 15 heating systems not meeting current definition; minimum 50 pct. renewable energy or waste heat required for classification as effective

numeric_thresholds.gates: Minimum renewable energy or waste heat share required for designation as effective district heating system (EED Art. 26.1 definition)

numeric_thresholds.gates: High CO2 price assumption for affald-reduction scenario (alternative scenario); triggers sensitivity analysis for waste heat economy

numeric_thresholds.gates: Baseline CO2 price (2020) used in cost-benefit calculations; referenced against 2030 and 2050 projections

numeric_thresholds.gates: Typical capital cost per MW investment for heat pump technology in cost-benefit model

numeric_thresholds.gates: Identified maximum technical surplus waste heat capacity available for district heating integration; 2.866 MW considered but 2.211 MW represents realistic economically viable segment

numeric_thresholds.gates: Net effective waste heat behaviour for district heating from combined heating systems (Scenario 0 baseline)

compliance_triggers.consequence: District heating system must integrate waste heat to qualify as effective heating under EED Art. 26.1; non-compliance triggers reclassification and potential subsidy withdrawal

compliance_triggers.consequence: DC operator may be subject to mandatory waste heat recovery feasibility assessment; affirmative assessment creates obligation to offer heat to district operator or third party

compliance_triggers.consequence: DC operators in areas with fossil affald plants must offset waste heat loss via alternative heat sources or face heating capacity shortfalls; triggers investment requirements for waste heat integration
compliance_triggers.applies_to: Both DC operator and municipal heat planning authority

compliance_triggers.condition: If CO2 price reaches 1500 kr./ton (scenario upper bound)
compliance_triggers.consequence: Cost-benefit economics shift dramatically in favour of waste heat recovery; previously marginal projects become economically viable, triggering mandatory implementation priority

compliance_triggers.consequence: Heat cannot be credited toward effective district heating designation; alternative renewable sources must be procured, increasing operational cost burden on heat off-taker

result.temperature_signals: The document does not contain explicit temperature thresholds or operating bands specific to data centre waste heat. However, heat pump integration assumptions (costs ranging 8000 DKK/kW) indicate acceptance of low-temperature waste heat (0-100 C range) for district heating via mechanical upgrade. The baseline fjernvarme cost-benefit model (384 kr./MWh for effective waste heat systems) reflects typical district heating inlet temperatures (60-80 C hot side after heat pump integration). For individual heat pump systems, marginal cost efficiency is highest at 173 kr./MWh (Scenario 0), suggesting economically viable recovery below 50 C from high-duty-cycle processes. No temperature grade differentiation (LowT/MidT/HighT manufacturing tiers) is defined; assessment treats all non-fossil waste heat as equivalent if achieving 50 pct. integration threshold.
result.transaction_cost_signals: Administrative burden is concentrated in the comprehensive assessment itself (multi-year cycle, scenario modeling, cost-benefit analysis per heating system type). Ongoing obligations include: (1) District heating operators must validate effective efficiency status every 5 years (50 pct. renewable/waste heat test); (2) Data centres receiving mandatory assessment letters must submit feasibility studies (estimated administrative cost: technical consulting, municipal coordination, contractual negotiation with heat offtakers); (3) Scenario 1 affald reduction policy triggers municipal heat planning updates and competitive bidding for waste heat contracts (metering, allocation of costs between operator and offtaker). No explicit permitting or certification regime is imposed, but cost-benefit economics create implicit gatekeeping: projects not meeting 200 kr./MWh total system cost threshold (Table 14 baseline) are deprioritized for public funding and grid priority. Contracting friction is high when multiple potential heat offtakers compete (Scenario 0 shows variation from 297-556 kr./MWh across 10 heating areas, indicating negotiation cost sensitivity to local supply-demand balance).
notable_quotes: Denne comprehensive assessment skal tages som en udydning til NECP'ens afsnit om varme- og klølesektoren og består af fire dele, der følger opgavebeskrivelsen fra bilag X i EED
Den gælende definition på effektive fjernvarme- og fjernkølelsystemer samt varmeplansomrader i Danmark
For en fjernvarmekunde (alternativ 2 og 3 overfor) vil det være de dyreste produktionsanlæg i det pågældende fjernvarmesystem, der står for at dække det marginale varmebehov

Det bemærkes, at der ikke er alle steder, hvor fjernvarme er en mulig varmeforsyning. Fjernvarme er rentabel i områder med høj bygningsttæthed, men af flere grunde kan ikke alle disse områder etablere en fjernvarmeledning eller øge deres eksisterende fjernvarmekapacitet

result.title: BS EN ISO 50001:2018+A1:2024 - Energy management systems — Requirements with guidance for use
result.summary: ISO 50001:2018+A1:2024 is an international energy management systems (EnMS) standard that specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and improving energy performance. It applies to any organization regardless of size or type, requiring systematic data-driven approach to achieve continual energy performance improvement through energy efficiency, energy use and energy consumption management.

key_articles.requirement: Organization must establish, implement, maintain and continually improve an EnMS including processes needed, their interactions, and continually improve energy performance in accordance with the document requirements

Top management shall demonstrate leadership and commitment with respect to continuous improvement of energy performance and effectiveness of EnMS by ensuring EnMS scope and boundaries are established; energy policy, objectives and targets are compatible with strategic direction; EnMS requirements are integrated into business processes; and action plans are approved and implemented

Top management shall establish an energy policy that is appropriate to organization purpose; provides framework for setting and reviewing objectives and targets; includes commitment to ensure availability of information and resources; includes commitment to satisfy legal requirements and other requirements; includes commitment to continuous improvement; supports procurement of efficient products and services; and supports design activities that consider energy performance improvement

Top management shall ensure responsibilities and authorities for relevant roles are assigned and communicated. Energy management team shall be responsible for: establishing, implementing and maintaining EnMS; ensuring conformity with requirements; implementing action plans; reporting on EnMS performance to top management; and establishing criteria and methods needed to ensure operation and control of EnMS are effective

Organization shall develop and conduct energy review. To develop energy review organization shall: analyze energy use and consumption based on measurement and data; identify current types of energy; evaluate past and current energy use(s) and consumption; based on analysis, identify SEUs; for each SEU determine relevant variables, current energy performance, and identify person(s) doing work that influence or affect SEUs; determine and prioritize opportunities for improving energy performance; estimate future energy use(s) and energy consumption. Energy review shall be updated at defined intervals and in response to major changes in facilities, equipment, systems or energy-using processes

Organization shall determine EnPIs that are appropriate for measuring and monitoring energy performance and enable organization to demonstrate energy performance improvement. Method for determining and updating EnPI shall be maintained as documented information. Where organization has data indicating relevant variables significantly affect energy performance, organization shall consider such data to establish appropriate EnPI(s)

Organization shall establish one or more energy baseline(s) using information from energy review taking into account suitable period of time. Where organization has data indicating relevant variables significantly affect energy performance, organization shall carry out normalization of EnPI value(s) and corresponding EnB(s). EnB(s) shall be revised if: EnPI(s) no longer reflect organization's energy performance; there have been major changes to static factors; according to pre-determined method. Organization shall retain information of EnB(s), relevant variable data and modifications to EnB(s) as documented information

key_articles.topic: Planning for Collection of Energy Data
key_articles.requirement: Organization shall ensure that key characteristics of operations affecting energy performance are identified, measured, monitored and analysed at planned intervals. Organization shall define and implement energy data collection plan appropriate to its size, complexity, resources and measurement and monitoring equipment. Plan shall specify data necessary to monitor key characteristics and state how and at what frequency data shall be collected and retained. Data to be collected shall include: relevant variables for SEUs; energy consumption related to SEUs and organization; operational criteria related to SEUs; static factors if applicable; data specified in action plans. Energy data collection plan shall be reviewed at defined intervals and updated as appropriate

Organization shall: determine necessary competence of person(s) doing work under its control that affects energy performance and EnMS; ensure these persons are competent on basis of appropriate education, training, skills or experience; where applicable, take actions to acquire necessary competence and evaluate effectiveness of actions taken; retain appropriate documented information as evidence of competence

Persons doing work under organization's control shall be aware of: energy policy; their contribution to effectiveness of EnMS including achievement of objectives and energy targets and benefits of improved energy performance; impact of their activities or behaviour with respect to energy performance; implications of not conforming with EnMS requirements

Organization shall determine internal and external communications relevant to EnMS. Organization shall establish and implement process by which any person(s) doing work under organization's control can make comments or suggest improvements to EnMS and energy performance. Organization shall consider retaining documented information of suggested improvements

Organization's EnMS shall include documented information required by document and determined by organization as necessary for effectiveness of EnMS and to demonstrate energy performance improvement. When creating and updating documented information organization shall ensure appropriate: identification and description (title, date, author, reference number); format (language, software version, graphics) and media (paper, electronic); review and approval for suitability and adequacy. Documented information shall be controlled to ensure: availability and suitability for use where and when needed; adequate protection (loss of confidentiality, improper use, loss of integrity)

Organization shall plan, implement and control processes related to its SEUs needed to meet requirements and to implement actions determined in 6.2 by: establishing criteria for processes including effective operation and maintenance of facilities, equipment, systems and energy-using processes where absence can lead to significant deviation from intended energy performance; communicating criteria to relevant person(s) doing work under organization's control; implementing control of processes in accordance with criteria including operating and maintaining facilities, equipment, systems and energy-using processes in accordance with established criteria; keeping documented information to extent necessary to have confidence processes have been carried out as planned. Organization shall control planned changes and review consequences of unintended changes, taking actions to mitigate any adverse effects

Organization shall consider energy performance improvement opportunities and operational control in design of new, modified and renovated facilities, equipment, systems and energy-using processes that can have significant impact on energy performance over planned or expected operating lifetime. Results of energy performance consideration shall be incorporated into specification, design and procurement activities. Organization shall retain documented information of design activities related to energy performance

Organization shall establish and implement criteria for evaluating energy performance over planned or expected operating lifetime when procuring energy using products, equipment and services which are expected to have significant impact on organization's energy performance. When procuring products, equipment and services that have or can have impact on SEUs, organization shall inform suppliers that energy performance is one of evaluation criteria for procurement. Organization shall define and communicate specifications for ensuring energy performance of procured equipment and services and purchase of energy

key_articles.topic: Monitoring, Measurement, Analysis and Evaluation of Energy Performance and EnMS
key_articles.requirement: Organization shall determine for energy performance and EnMS: what needs to be monitored and measured (at minimum: effectiveness of action plans in achieving objectives and energy targets; EnPI(s); operation of SEUs; actual versus expected energy consumption); methods for monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation to ensure valid results; when monitoring and measurement shall be performed; when results shall be analysed and evaluated. Organization shall evaluate its energy performance and effectiveness of EnMS. Improvement in energy performance shall be evaluated by comparing EnPI value(s) against corresponding EnB(s). result.temperature_signals: The document establishes a comprehensive temperature-tiered framework for waste heat recovery feasibility across six bands: (1) Very Low Temperature (20-40 °C) for ventilation systems suitable for warm water preheating and heating pumps; (2) Low Temperature (40-90 °C) for process facilities, drying systems, and cooling water, enabling service water heating 75-125 °C and cooling generation 80-160 °C; (3) Medium Temperature (100-150 °C) from steam generation plants for preheating and process heating; (4) Medium-High Temperature (125-400 °C) from combustion air preheating enabling electricity generation via ORC-processes at 70-450 °C band; (5) High Temperature (150-600 °C) from furnace combustion fumes enabling steam-process electricity generation at 250-540 °C or direct district heating supply at 90+ °C threshold. The framework shows temperature is the primary gating factor for technology selection: lower bands (under 90 °C) gate district heating and absorption cooling; medium bands (100-150 °C) enable ORC and preheating; high bands (250+ °C) enable steam turbine electricity generation. Case studies validate: ice hockey stadium recovers 20-120 °C ammonia-water heat; London Underground operates steady-state 75 °C district heating supply from ventilation waste; Schuler metal factory extracts 600 °C furnace fumes yielding 1000 MWh/year with 1.58-year payback, demonstrating high-temperature sources unlock fastest investment returns.
result.transaction_cost_signals: The brochure frames decision-making and investment barriers through six toolbox elements addressing transaction costs: (1) Investment Decision Support section notes decision-making is a "challenging issue for potential investors" and the DSS tool is required to "inform first steps of investment decision making process"; (2) Permits section explicitly states need to navigate "relevant procedural requirements and national regulations (such as acts of parliament, statutory provisions, government regulations as well as ministerial and local ordinances) related to waste heat investment implementation"; (3) Funding section identifies need for "financial resources and business model construction for investment" requiring specific toolbox guidance on business model development; (4) Policy section notes regulatory variation across European regions requiring navigation of both "European Union Policy" and "National Policy" frameworks; (5) Decision Support System section outputs "pre-feasibility study useful also for policy makers to define which incentive schemes should be developed to make waste heat recovering an attractive investment"; (6) Regional Implementation Manuals section structured around Funding Opportunities, Business Plans and Business Models, and Permits as distinct administrative burdens. Case examples highlight administrative burden impact: Manner Wafers Vienna required "local grid modernization in less than a year" for connection; Shipyard Viktor Lenac achieved "very short payback period of less than 2 years" suggesting permitting and contracting friction is recoverable through high-temperature sources. The platform itself (www.waste-heat.eu) functions as a transaction-cost reduction tool providing centralized access to regional cadasters, permit procedures, and funding databases for seven European regions.

result.temperature_signals: "Article 26 waste-heat recovery provisions do not specify explicit temperature bands but reference 'useful temperature level' and cooling system solutions 'allowing removing or capturing waste heat at useful temperature level with minimal ancillary energy inputs' (Art. 26(7), final paragraph). District heating/cooling systems are implicitly LowT/MidT compatible given focus on waste heat and renewable energy integration. No specific temperature thresholds (e.g., 30°C, 50°C, 70°C) are defined in the directive text; industrial and service facility thresholds are purely energy-based (MW) not temperature-based. Data centre waste-heat assessment must include 'technical feasibility and cost-efficiency' but does not mandate or exclude any specific exhaust temperature range.
result.transaction_cost_signals: Article 26(7) explicitly requires cost-benefit analysis as a mandatory compliance mechanism for DCs exceeding 1 MW - this is a core transaction cost driver: data collection, expert assessment, documentation, competent authority review, and potential permit applications. Article 12 reporting obligations (500 kW+ DCs annually) impose data collection, aggregation, and disclosure burdens with potential confidentiality disputes. Article 25 heating/cooling assessments require stakeholder participation, public availability of plans, and administrative coordination across regional/local authorities. Article 11 energy management systems and audits (enterprises >85 TJ and >10 TJ respectively) create ongoing certification, monitoring, and reporting obligations. Exemptions from Art. 26(7) (geological storage sites, peak-load facilities, district heating connections) reduce transaction costs conditionally. Member States must establish 'transparent, non-discriminatory criteria' for cost assessment (Art. 26(7)), adding procedural burden. Commission authority to review and propose legislative changes (Art. 33, Art. 35) introduces regulatory uncertainty and re-assessment costs."

result.title: Data Center Waste Heat for District Heating Networks: A Review
result.summary: This peer-reviewed journal article systematically reviews the integration of data center waste heat (DCWHR) into district heating (DH) networks globally. It examines technical feasibility, energy efficiency, economic viability, and environmental impacts across multiple case studies (Europe, China, Nordic regions). The paper defines waste heat temperature bands from DC cooling systems and establishes temperature requirements for DH integration via heat pumps, thermal storage, and 4GDH/5GDH systems. It serves as a comprehensive technical reference for temperature-dependent heat recovery feasibility and lifecycle assessment of DCWHR projects.

Table 2 provides detailed breakdown of market share and recovery ranking by temperature grade.

result.temperature_signals: "DC Waste Heat Supply Temperature Bands (defining LowT/MidT/HighT tiers): LowT (low-grade, <30°C) includes CRAC return water 15–20°C, CRAH return air 25–47°C (practical range ~25–30°C for water), HE return water 20–30°C, two-phase return air 20–40°C. These require substantial heat pump uplift (COP 3–5) to reach DH supply temperatures and represent recovery rankings 3rd–5th, smallest market share. MidT (medium-grade, 30–50°C) includes two-phase condenser coolant upper range 40–50°C and emerging hybrid systems; feasible for integration but requires moderate heat pump boost. HighT (high-grade, 50–60°C) includes liquid-side server/back-level cooling return water 50–60°C; represents highest recovery ranking (1st), largest technical potential, and enables direct or near-direct integration to 4GDH supply (50–60°C) or 5GDH with minimal heat pump assist or none required. DH Integration Thresholds: 1GDH supply 90–110°C incompatible with any DC waste grade without major HP cost; 2GDH (80–90°C) requires HP uplift even from highest-grade DC waste; 3GDH (70–80°C) feasible but costly; 4GDH (50–60°C supply, 25°C return) matches HighT DC output and represents inflection point where DCWHR becomes economically viable without extreme operational burden; 5GDH further reduces supply/return and enhances efficiency. Heat Pump Role: HP COP 3–5 enables transformation of LowT waste (15–30°C) to DH supply (50–70°C) but at significant operational energy cost; payback 6–15 years typical. For MidT and HighT, COP improves and payback shortens. Thermal Energy Storage (TES): 80–96% cycle efficiency enables buffering of continuous DC waste (70–170 TWh annual global, 35–85 TWh recoverable) against seasonal DH demand, critical for system feasibility in northern climates with winter-peak heating."
result.transaction_cost_signals: "Infrastructure Investment: DC DCWHR projects require substantial initial capital (payback 6–15 years typical), heat pump equipment procurement, TES installation, heat exchangers, piping integration, and connection to DH networks. Metering & Monitoring: Systems must meter DC waste heat output, DH supply/return temperatures, flow rates, and heat pump performance (COP) to validate contractual heat delivery and billing. Heat pump controls require real-time monitoring. Permits & Approvals: DH network connection requires coordination with municipal utilities, thermal network operator approval, environmental review, and technical standards compliance (4GDH vs. legacy DH). Connection agreements between DC operator and DH entity. Certification & Standards: Compliance with DH generation standards (4GDH, 5GDH classifications); heat exchanger/pump equipment certification; energy efficiency declarations. Data Requirements: Cooling system waste heat characterization (temperature, flow, volume) for DH matching; building heating demand profiles for sizing HP/TES; utility-level coordination data for load balancing. Operational Burden: 24/7 DC waste heat continuous availability vs. seasonal DH demand creates dispatch complexity; TES operation adds control burden; heat pump controls require expertise. System Coordination: DC operator (electricity-driven cooling) and DH operator (heat sales) require contractual alignment on temperature, flow, priority (cooling reliability vs. heat export), and revenue sharing. Risk allocation for operational disparity (DC cooling takes priority if conflict arises). Environmental Audits: Lifecycle assessment; GHG emissions reduction verification (typical 3–50 % reductions claimed across cases); carbon accounting methodology standardization needed (inconsistencies noted in literature). Feasibility Studies: Energy, economic, environmental (3E) analysis mandatory for project viability assessment; modeling of heat pump COP, TES efficiency, seasonal demand; sensitivity to utility incentives and heat pricing. Regulatory Compliance: National/local energy efficiency mandates; waste heat recovery targets (e.g., EU directives, national acts) for large energy-consuming installations; connection to Directive 2012/27/EU or equivalents on energy efficiency. Government Incentives: Subsidies, tax credits, district heating expansion support; critical for project financial viability (noted as influencing factor in feasibility)."

result.summary: This Italian decree updates the White Certificates (Certificati Bianchi / TEE) mechanism for the 2025-2030 period. It establishes mandatory energy efficiency obligations for electricity and gas distribution companies, specifying eligible interventions (grouped by industrial, network, services, and behavioral sectors), lifetime coefficients, and energy savings targets. Two methods available: (a) consumptive method per program of measure as per Art. 1, cap. 1; (b) standardized method per program as per Art. 1, cap. 2.

result.title: Decreto Ministeriale 21 maggio 2021 - Determinazione degli obiettivi quantitativi nazionali di risparmio energetico per il periodo 2021-2024 (white certificates)
result.summary: This Italian ministerial decree of May 21, 2021, establishes the national quantitative energy savings targets for white certificates (Certificati Bianchi) covering 2021-2024. It defines obligations for electricity and gas distributors, methods for valuing and certifying energy efficiency projects, and procedures for recognizing energy savings through standardized (PS) and customized (PC) projects. The decree explicitly mentions heating networks (teleriscaldamento) and cooling systems as eligible projects but does not specifically address data centre waste heat recovery or district heating from data centres.

key_articles.requirement: Modifies the 2017 decree to extend applicability. Sets the framework for determining national quantitative energy savings targets (certificati bianchi) for the 2021-2024 period.
Establishes specific energy savings objectives per year: 0.45 million white certificates (2021); 0.75 million (2022); 1.05 million (2023); 1.08 million (2024).

key_articles.topic: Quantitative national objectives and related obligations for 2021-2024
key_articles.requirement: Details the mechanism of white certificates, their emission and tracking. TEP (Tonnellate Equivalenti di Petrolio) is the unit of account.
Allows temporary associations of companies and mandates to conduct energy efficiency measures. Requires specific contract types and delegation for implementation.

key_articles.topic: Requirements and limits for white certificates
key_articles.requirement: Specifies that energy efficiency projects must be classified into typologies. Certificates issued must follow a standardized model. GSE (Gestore dei Servizi Energetici) validates projects in collaboration with ENEA and RSE.

key_articles.topic: Base case (asta) system for white certificates
key_articles.requirement: Introduces 'asta' mechanism to determine white certificate value, incentivizing energy efficiency measures. References PNIEC (Piano Nazionale Integrato per l'Energia e il Clima) and monitoring by FIRE/GSE.

key_articles.topic: Procedures for evaluation and certification of energy savings
key_articles.requirement: GSE evaluates projects in collaboration with FIRE (Federazione Italiana per l'uso Razionale dell'Energia) and certifies according to UNI CEI standards (UNI CEI 11352, 11339, ISO 50001). Requires preliminary approval.

key_articles.topic: Emission of white certificates from energy efficiency projects
key_articles.requirement: Prohibits certificates from import if cost exceeds 15 euro and adjusts by 60% of duty if competing with favourable duty rates. References PNIEC and climate action standards.
Specifies monitoring for COVID-19 impacts and operational continuity. Requires documentation of baseline conditions, consumption analysis, and ex ante/ex post monitoring per Allegato 1.

Establishes two methods: PC (customized projects, evaluated on-site) and PS (standardized projects). Requires baseline measurement over 12 months and ex ante/ex post monitoring with representative parameters.

key_articles.topic: Modalities for recognition of white certificates (Allegato 2)
key_articles.requirement: Defines four types of white certificates (Type I-IV) based on primary energy savings from electricity and natural gas reduction. All certificates denominated per TEP; commercial dimension is 1 TEP minimum.

result.temperature_signals: The decree does not specify temperature bands or process temperature thresholds for low/medium/high temperature manufacturing. It applies uniformly to energy efficiency measures across all sectors (civil, transport, heating networks) without distinguishing by supply temperature. Heating networks (teleriscaldamento) are mentioned as eligible but no temperature grade differentiation (low-temp < 80 C, mid-temp 80-120 C, high-temp > 120 C) is provided in the text.
result.transaction_cost_signals: Administrative burden is significant: (1) GSE preliminary validation (RVP) with 24-30 month turnaround; (2) baseline monitoring requirement of 12 months minimum before project submission; (3) ex ante/ex post measurement and monitoring data collection (daily or monthly frequency); (4) technical documentation in standardized format per Allegato 1 (describing systems, algorithms, baseline reconstruction, consumption parameters); (5) UNI CEI certification by qualified laboratory per Art. 8 (adds cost for accreditation); (6) for customized projects (PC), GSE collaboration with ENEA/RSE for on-site validation; (7) annual/biennial reporting to GSE on monitoring results; (8) proof of project implementation (photos, invoices, work certificates per Allegato 1); (9) compliance with baseline privacy and data confidentiality requirements (Art. 18-bis). Certification must be renewed or revalidated within 12 months post-implementation. Total time to white certificate issuance typically 24-36 months from project initiation to final GSE recognition.

result.title: Denmark's Draft Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP)
result.summary: Denmark's Draft NECP (submitted 31 December 2018) establishes national targets for heating and cooling decarbonization, with a binding commitment that at least 90% of district heating consumption must be based on energy sources other than coal, oil or gas by 2030. The plan allocates 13.4 million EUR annually for promotion of waste heat use in district heating from 2020 onwards. It sets renewable energy trajectories of 55% by 2030 and commits to climate neutrality by 2050 under the Paris Agreement.

From 2020, 13.4 million EUR/year is earmarked for promotion of use of waste heat in district heating

55% renewable energy share in gross final energy consumption by 2030; trajectory milestone: 42% by 2020
Renewable electricity share expected to exceed 100% of consumption by 2030
Annual target of 0.8% end-use energy savings; Cumulative savings 2021-2030: 271.7 PJ (55 × 4.94%)
Denmark aims for climate-neutral society by 2050 with net zero emissions in EU and Denmark by 2050

result.title: Denmark's Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (Final NECP)
result.summary: Denmark's Final NECP (December 2019) establishes legally binding targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 70% by 2030 (relative to 1990) and achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. The plan mandates at least 80% of district heating to be based on renewable sources by 2030 and 59.9% renewable share in heating/cooling sector. It addresses waste heat utilization, district heating integration, biomass sustainability, heat pump deployment, and energy efficiency improvements across all sectors.

key_articles.requirement: Denmark commits to 70% reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 relative to 1990 levels, with net-zero by 2050. ESR regulation requires 39% reduction in non-ETS emissions by 2030 vs. 2005 baseline.
At least 80% of district heating consumption shall be based on renewable energy sources or waste heat by 2030. Estimated renewable share in heating/cooling sector to reach 59.9% by 2030.
Share of renewables in heating and cooling sector currently 54%, expected to increase to 59.9% by 2030 via biomass, heat pumps, and solar thermal deployment.
Denmark's cumulative target for 2021-2030 is 55 times annual target of 0.8% of average final energy consumption (610.3 PJ), totaling 268.5 PJ or 6414 ktoe cumulative savings.

Energy saving requirements for all public sector buildings under article 5 of EED. Competitive subsidy scheme for private building renovation (300 mDKK/year 2021-2024); efficiency of existing buildings to be increased through building code requirements.

Danish heating demand covered primarily by district heating (65% of households), with remainder supplied by natural gas, individual heat generation, and phase-out of oil burners. Large-scale deployment of solar thermal plants, heat pumps, geothermal energy, and surplus heat utilization are measures to enable heating sector integration and flexibility.
Electricity generation from renewables to exceed 100% by 2030; at least 90% of district heating to be based on energy sources other than coal, oil or gas by 2030.

Voluntary Danish industry agreement on sustainable biomass (concluded 2014): 90% of biomass used in district heat and electricity production must be sustainable and documented; applies to plants with capacity above 20 MW.

More than half of bioenergy consumption in Denmark used for district heating and electricity production. Waste (bio-degradable) share expected as contribution source for heating sector alongside biomass and heat pumps.

Significant increase of heat pumps in heating sector for both district heating and individual heat production expected to contribute to more flexible energy system and integration with electricity sector.

result.title: EcoDataCenter in Falun secures a future power supply of 80 MW from renewable sources
result.summary: EcoDataCenter in Falun operates a waste-heat recovery system with Falu Energi & Vatten (FEV), a municipal energy company. The facility recovers surplus heat from the data center for use in district heating and biofuel production. A 2022 investment of SEK 50 million secured 80 MW of renewable electricity capacity, enabling facility expansion and increased waste-heat recovery volumes. The arrangement demonstrates a public-private model for DC waste-heat integration into municipal district heating infrastructure.

result.title: Optimal framework for integrated energy system considering carbon emission-green certificate mutual offsetting mechanism and multiple energy prices impacting
result.summary: This research paper proposes an integrated energy system (IES) optimization framework for China that considers mutual offsetting between carbon emission quotas and green certificates under a multi-market linkage mechanism. It models how prices in electricity, coal, natural gas, and carbon/green certificate markets interact to influence renewable energy deployment, carbon emission reduction, and overall system costs. The framework does not focus specifically on data centre waste heat recovery but addresses broader energy system integration with certificate trading mechanics relevant to incentive design.

result.title: EU AI Act High-Level Overview (Future of Life Institute 2024)
result.summary: This is a high-level overview of the EU AI Act published by the Future of Life Institute, summarizing the Act's risk-based classification scheme (unacceptable, prohibited, high-risk, and minimal risk categories), obligations for AI providers and deployers across different risk tiers, and governance arrangements through the AI Office. The document does not address data centre waste-heat recovery, district heating, or thermal efficiency; relevance is minimal.

key_articles.requirement: Prohibits AI systems deploying subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques; exploiting vulnerabilities; social scoring; criminal risk assessment based solely on profiling; facial recognition database compilation; emotion inference in workplaces/educational institutions; biometric categorisation systems; and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement (with limited exceptions).

Defines high-risk AI systems as those used as a safety component in EU-regulated products/laws requiring third-party conformity assessment, or those under Annex III use cases (unless performing narrow procedural tasks, improving prior human activity, detecting decision deviations without replacing human assessment, or preparatory assessment tasks).

High-risk providers must establish a risk management system, conduct data governance, draw up technical documentation, design systems for record-keeping and human oversight, ensure accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, and establish a quality management system.
GPAI models are considered systemic when cumulative compute used for training is greater than 10^25 floating point operations per second (FLOPS).
Providers must notify the Commission if their GPAI model meets systemic criteria within 2 weeks of entry into force.

All GPAI model providers must draw up technical documentation, provide documentation to downstream providers, establish Copyright Directive compliance policy, and publish sufficiently detailed summary of training content used.

Providers of systemic-risk GPAI models must perform model evaluations including adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, track and report serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensure adequate cybersecurity protection.

Codes of practice will account for international approaches and identify type/nature of systemic risks and risk management modalities, with AI Office inviting GPAI providers, national competent authorities, civil society, industry, academia, and downstream providers to participate.
Downstream providers can lodge complaints regarding upstream provider infringement to the AI Office.

key_articles.topic: AI Office investigation of systemic risks
key_articles.requirement: The AI Office may conduct product evaluations of GPAI models and investigate systemic risks, particularly following qualified reports from scientific panel of independent experts.
The AI Office may assess compliance where information gathered under its request powers is insufficient, and investigate systemic risks following qualified expert panel reports.

result.title: Feasibility of Data Centre Waste Heat Recovery for Industrial Space Heating: Turkey Case Study
result.summary: This technical case study evaluates the feasibility of integrating data centre waste heat into district heating networks for industrial space heating in Turkey. Using MATLAB-based simulation of the TOFAS automotive production facility, the study quantifies annual heat recovery potential (78,358 kWh), economic viability (66.3-year payback period, 1.51% ROI), and environmental benefits (15,671 kg CO2 reduction). The research demonstrates technical feasibility through energy flow analysis but identifies economic constraints and seasonal mismatches that limit near-term deployment without optimized conditions.

Annual savings computed via total available waste heat cost displacement; capital investment estimated at EUR 500,000; operating costs at EUR 5,000/year; economic viability assessed through cumulative ROI and payback period calculations.
CO2 emissions abatement calculated by multiplying available waste heat by emission factor of fuel displaced (electricity 0.2310 kg CO2eq/kWh); total annual CO2 reduction estimated at 15,671 kg.

(4) No temperature-grade classification (low/medium/high °C) is provided, limiting direct mapping to industrial process heating tiers (LowT/MidT/HighT). The case implicitly demonstrates that DC cooling air exhaust (typically 30-45°C unspecified here) is marginal for direct district heating without supplemental heating or pre-treatment, a finding relevant to low-temperature industrial space heating applications but not explicitly quantified.

The document establishes a multi-tier temperature grading system critical for DC waste heat utilization feasibility:

LowT (below 30°C): Typical air-cooled DC waste heat (30-35°C return temperature). Requires aggressive heat pump uplift (~35-55°C) to reach DH supply standards. High electricity penalty; COP ~3-3.5 typical; economic viability marginal unless electricity prices very low or heat sales revenue subsidized. Covers most existing Nordic DCs without infrastructure upgrade.

MidT (30-60°C): Liquid-cooled DC systems or hybrid cooling; practical operational range 50-60°C capture temperature. Reduces heat pump duty; COP improvement enables positive economics. Yandex operational winter supply ~68°C demonstrates this tier achieves near-DH-supply temperatures without extreme heat pump penalty. This tier unlocks commercial viability for waste heat reuse in Nordic region.

HighT (60-75°C): Direct supply feasible or minimal heat pump uplift. Liquid cooling optimized for heat recovery. Only achievable with design-phase infrastructure choices (liquid cooling, server-room heat recovery). Not represented in current deployed Nordic DCs; future opportunity if industry adopts high-temperature cooling design.

Supply temperature to DH network: 75°C target (Helsinki standard); return 40-70°C seasonal variation. Winter return water warmer (DH demand high, shorter residence time), summer return cooler. This asymmetry means same DC waste heat supply provides more leverage in winter (steeper ΔT for heat pump) vs. summer (lower marginal ΔT gain); DH operator economics and DC operator incentives diverge seasonally.

Practical implication: Nordic DCs currently deliver LowT grade; transition to MidT via liquid cooling is primary lever for unlocking economically viable waste heat integration. HighT remains aspirational/future-focused.
result.transaction_cost_signals:
The document identifies significant transaction costs and administrative friction in DC waste heat projects:

Contractual Complexity: DC-DH operator agreements must specify heat quality (temperature stability), quantity (volume guarantees), pricing mechanism, duration, and responsibility for variation. "Transparent contracting" explicitly required but rarely achieved; both parties fear information disclosure (DC operator confidentiality on workload, DH operator confidentiality on pricing flexibility). Long-term supply contracts (10-20 years) standard to justify HP equipment investment, but lock in price risk for both parties.

Investment Payback Uncertainty: Heat recovery equipment investment (~€1-3M for typical 10 MW DC based on table references) requires 5-15 year payback horizon. Uncertainty over: electricity prices (major driver), fuel prices (competing heat source), DC workload stability (seasonal/interannual variation), DH demand (influenced by building efficiency codes, customer preferences), regulatory changes (renewable energy subsidies, emission limits). This uncertainty delays project approvals.

Regulatory Approval & Permitting: DH network connection requires municipal coordination; DC energy efficiency certification (ISO 14001 mentioned); potential zoning/environmental permits. Document does not quantify approval timeline but indicates it is "considerable" (see Forum/Ericsson projects mentioned as years-long approval process). Added cost of consultants, lawyers, environmental assessment.

Metering & Monitoring Burden: Supply quality (temperature, flow, pressure) must be continuously monitored; billing systems require metering accuracy. Document notes: "both parties need transparent data" but "DC operator very reluctant to share workload data." Separate metering infrastructure, control systems, and data handling protocols add ongoing operational cost.

Knowledge Barriers: "Most DC operators lack know-how" for heat recovery technical design; limited vendor competition for specialized HP+DH integration equipment in Nordic region; DH operators unfamiliar with DC heat supply dynamics. Each project requires bespoke engineering study; no standardized templates.

Business Model Risk: Question of who captures value (DC operator vs. DH operator) unresolved. Document states: "ownership of DCs varies; some DC operators invest, some DH operators invest, some jointly." Revenue split ambiguous—if DH operator purchases heat at wholesale, DC operator margin compressed; if DC operator negotiates premium for "green heat," DH operator resists. This friction raises negotiation time & cost.

Seasonal Mismatch Penalty: Heat supply-demand mismatch (high summer, low winter for DCs; inverse for DH) requires either: (1) thermal storage investment (adds €0.5-2M capex), (2) demand-side management (raises coordination cost), or (3) price penalties for imbalance (ongoing transaction cost). Document notes Yandex & TeliaCo solutions include this complexity but exact cost not quantified.

Reputational/Liability Risk: DC operators concerned waste heat reuse may be characterized as "waste" rather than "valuable" in consumer/political discourse; liability if heat quality fails and DH customers lose service; DH operators concerned DC workload volatility may destabilize network. Risk mitigation (insurance, redundancy) adds cost.

Total estimated transaction cost for Nordic DC-DH integration project: Not explicitly quantified, but document references "considerable investment" and "long approval timelines" suggesting €0.5-5M upfront (beyond equipment) plus ongoing governance cost ~5-10% of annual heat revenue.
notable_quotes: The two most important issues in waste heat utilization are heat demand and profitability. There must be a certain demand for heat in the near vicinity of the DC. Heat cannot be distributed long distances as efficiently as electricity.

Waste heat utilization with HPs in a DH network will affect the economics of the DC. Utilization requires investments in HP equipment, piping, and connection to the DH network. In addition, HP uses electricity to prime the heat, and thus it increases electricity consumption, which further increases the operational costs.

Upgrading DC cooling heat to DH temperatures are the differences between the HP COP and the cooling efficiency between cooling to ambient air and to DH temperatures. In the worst case it can be assumed, for simplicity's sake, that the cooling air or water from the DC and 75°C is the required minimum DH water temperature.

The potential for waste heat utilization from DCs was analyzed by conducting a literature review on cooling technologies and solutions for waste heat utilization. In addition, some of the most interesting projects currently related to DC waste heat utilization in the Nordic countries are analyzed through available online sources and literature.

result.summary: This research paper presents the Pan-European Thermal Atlas (version 4) developed under the Heat Roadmap Europe project.
