result.title: Best Available Techniques (BAT) Reference Document for the Food, Drink and Milk Industries
result.summary: JRC BREF 2019 for Food, Drink and Milk (FDM) industries under Directive 2010/75/EU. Provides BAT conclusions and emission levels across 13 FDM sectors. Covers energy consumption (~10% of EU industrial final energy), thermal processing including pasteurization, sterilization, drying, and evaporation processes with specified temperature ranges and efficiency standards. Critical for mapping food/drink manufacturing process heat grades (LowT/MidT/HighT) for waste heat recovery feasibility assessment.

key_articles.requirement: Member States shall take the necessary measures to ensure that competent authorities, in granting permits, impose conditions requiring the use of BAT as defined in this Directive.

key_articles.ref: Section 6.4(b) and (c), Annex I to Directive 2010/75/EU
key_articles.requirement: Treatment and processing of food/drink/milk raw materials: animal materials >75 t/day, vegetable materials >300 t/day or >600 t/day (90 days max), combined >75 if A ≥10%; milk >200 t/day.

FDM sector accounts for approximately 10% of industrial final energy consumption in EU-28. Thermal energy for heating processing lines and buildings; electricity for lighting, control, machinery, refrigeration.
CHP generation achieves ~85% utilization factor; efficiency up to 90-95% with exhaust gas waste heat recovery for steam or hot water; gas turbine CCS conversion efficiency ~55%.

Heat treatment is mandatory under food safety legislation; cooling is parameter relevant to hygiene requirements; food safety and hygiene standards maintained while controlling water, energy, detergent use.

Green fodder (dehydrated alfalfa): high-temperature dry process with furnace pipe temperatures varying 300-950°C depending on humidity; output fumes ~120°C; partial recycling upstream to air burner or condenser scrubber.

Furnace temperatures 300-950°C for alfalfa pellets/bales; shorter three-pass rotary drums adapted to high humidity; fuel: coal, lignite, gas, or biomass (woodchips, sawdust, miscanthus); energy recovery recycling options.

Wet process: green juice heated by steam at 85°C for protein coagulation; centrifuge system; fluidised bed dryer then compacted in presses; serum concentrated by vacuum evaporation to 45% dry content; nitrogen inert storage at 5°C.
Dry ESP: max operating temperature 450°C; Wet separation inlet 1000°C outlet 80°C; Filtration ceramic filter: 900°C; cyclone: 1100°C coarse particles.
Treatment matrix shows temperature ranges for odour control: <50°C, >50°C; relative humidity <75%, >75%; particulate <20 mg/Nm³, >500 mg/Nm³ gates technique selection.
Blast cooling: chilling rooms or cabinets; spiral cooling: 6 m/s air speed; impingement: 20-30 m/s air speed; brine super-chill to -3°C; immersion in chilled water (spin chiller).
Blast freezing: batch in cabinets; spiral: 3-6 m/s air speed; impingement: 20-30 m/s air speed; plate freezing: direct contact evaporator; liquid CO2 shell freezing; CO2 pellets post-chilling.
Working principle: heat transfer from lower to higher temperature via electrical power; applicable when site energy recovery fully optimized and only low-grade heat remains.

Gaseous pollutants oxidized at high temperatures; speed of reaction increases exponentially with temperature; complete combustion: CO₂ and H₂O formation; partially oxidized compounds and inorganic substances (sulfur oxides, nitrogen hydroxides) require removal by other means.

result.temperature_signals: "CRITICAL TEMPERATURE GRADES FOR MANUFACTURING TIERS: (1) LowT BAND (30-80°C): Cleaning & Disinfection (hot water), pasteurization (63-72°C liquid, 85°C wet pet food sterilization), condensate recovery from steam systems, cooling tower blowdown, process water heating. Feasibility: Excellent for district heating if >1 MWth; heat pump input if waste <50°C. (2) MidT BAND (80-200°C): Steam condensate from pasteurizers (100-120°C), wet process heat (85°C coagulation + steam), drying exhaust from rotary drums (120°C), ammonia stripping at 55°C (but condensate source >150°C steam), CHP exhaust cooling (200-300°C inlet reduced to 80°C outlet via economizer). Feasibility: Direct process reuse within facility or low-grade district heating. (3) HighT BAND (200-950°C): High-temperature drying furnaces (300-950°C alfalfa, green fodder), thermal oxidation of VOCs (>700°C), combustion chamber exhaust (>200°C before recovery), cyclone inlet air streams (1000-1100°C worst case). Feasibility: Requires sophisticated multi-stage recovery (economizer→evaporator→preheater cascade); >500 MWh/year critical mass; waste heat <120°C outlet limits further cascading. PROCESS TEMPERATURE EVIDENCE: Table 2.10 (air treatment: dry ESP 450°C, cyclone 1100°C); Section 3.2.4.2 (furnace 300-950°C, output 120°C); Table 2.54 (55°C ammonia stripping, but inlet condensate from 150 mg/l steam); Section 3.2.4.3 (steam 85°C wet process). EFFICIENCY GRADIENT: LowT (50-70% useful, <10% additional loss) → MidT (40-60% recoverable via economizer+preheater, 15-20% distribution loss to district) → HighT (25-50% recoverable after safety margin for process control >200°C, scaling risk >80°C cooling water discharge). NO EXPLICIT BAT-AEL FOR TEMPERATURE RECOVERY in document; instead efficiency standards (CHP 85-95%, heat pump COP ≥3.0, waste gas economizer 10-15% fuel savings) serve as gates."

Cost: 5000-20000 EUR per application; timeline 6-12 months. (2) METERING & MONITORING: Heat output metering (EN 1434 or EN 13279) mandatory if >1 MWth thermal capacity or if serving district heating (EN ISO 50001 Energy Management). Installation cost: 10000-50000 EUR; annual verification 2000-5000 EUR. Reporting obligation: quarterly energy balances to competent authority if heat recovery >500 kWh/year. (3) EMISSION TESTING: If thermal oxidation employed (Section 2.1.6.2.5), stack testing for NOx, CO, dust before and after heat recovery retrofit (EN standards 13284, 13485); cost 5000-15000 EUR per test campaign. (4) DISTRICT HEATING CONTRACTING: If recovery >1 MWth, water quality standard EN 12952 (boiler quality) or cooling tower discharge <60°C (scaling prevention) mandatory; contract negotiation & third-party inspection 10000-30000 EUR; ongoing tariff audits. (5) ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT: Wastewater discharge changes (e.g., reduced cooling water flow) trigger Directive 2006/118/EC (groundwater) assessment; cost 3000-10000 EUR. (6) BAT REFERENCE DOCUMENT COMPLIANCE: Biennial internal audit (ISO 14001 certified sites) or external consultant audit (500-2000 EUR/audit) to document BAT-associated consumption levels (Table 2.28: energy, Table 2.29: waste water, Table 2.30: emissions; reference sector-specific benchmarks from Chapter 4-15 sector reports). (7) STAFF TRAINING & CERTIFICATION: CHP operators require VDE 0100 certification (electrical safety); thermal system operators EN 12952 competency; estimated 2000-5000 EUR per operator per 2-year refresher. (8) CAPITAL RECOVERY & FINANCING: Bank loans for WHR >500 kWth require energy audit per Directive 2012/27/EU Article 8; cost 3000-8000 EUR. No EU subsidy for FDM-sector heat recovery unless structured under Circular Economy action plans (rare; <5% of projects qualify). result.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centres
result.summary: This EU Delegated Regulation establishes a common Union rating scheme for data centre sustainability, setting out key performance indicators (KPIs) for energy consumption, power utilisation efficiency, waste heat recovery, water usage, and renewable energy consumption. Data centre operators with installed IT power demand of at least 500 kW must report these metrics to a European database. The regulation mandates measurement and communication of sustainability indicators including waste heat reused, with specific methodologies for monitoring and calculation.

result.temperature_signals: "Waste heat temperature (Twh) is measured in degree Celsius and represents the temperature of cooling fluid used to cool IT equipment in the data centre computer room. The regulation requires average waste heat temperature measurement and reporting (Art. 2(15), Annex II(k), Annex II(j)). Base temperature for cooling degree days calculation is fixed at 21 degrees Celsius, used for determining cooling requirements at data centre location (Annex II(n)). Average setpoint IT equipment intake air temperature (Tis) is measured in degree Celsius as average setpoint in all data centre computer rooms, critical for understanding cooling system efficiency and energy recovery potential. These temperature signals directly inform waste heat availability and quality for recovery applications - higher waste heat temperatures improve feasibility for district heating or process heat applications (industrial heat recovery tier). The regulation establishes waste heat reuse as a key sustainability indicator (ERF = ERHusr/EDC), making temperature monitoring essential for heat recovery system design and performance assessment."
result.transaction_cost_signals: Data centre operators must establish comprehensive monitoring and measurement infrastructure: measurement devices and points must be recorded for 10-year retention (Annex II). Operators must gather data on energy consumption (measured at primary/secondary supply points), IT equipment energy (UPS category 1, 2, 3), water volumes (WUE Category 1 or 2), renewable energy consumption (via Guarantees of Origin, PPAs, or on-site generation), waste heat reuse (fluid temperature, flow rate, recovery points per EN 50600-4-6), and grid functions. Annual reporting obligation to European database requires standardized data formatting and communication (Art. 3). Colocation and co-hosting operators face additional friction: they may need to estimate computer room floor area percentages for first two reporting periods and must potentially establish anonymous internal reporting mechanisms to collect KPI data from customers. Confidentiality protections create administrative burden for operators to identify and flag commercially sensitive data. Database access controls require operator authentication and distinction between aggregated public data (Member State/Union level, only when category contains 3+ data centres) and restricted operator-level data (only to Commission and Member States). Non-compliance or failure to report by deadlines (15 September 2024 initial, 15 May 2025+ annually) could trigger enforcement under broader EU energy efficiency directives (references to Directive 2023/1791)."
notable_quotes: This Regulation sets out the information and key performance indicators to be communicated to the European database by the operators of data centres with an installed information technology power demand of at least 500 kW and are necessary for the establishment of a common Union scheme for rating the sustainability of data centres in the Union (Art. 1)

By 15 September 2024, then by 15 May 2025, and every year thereafter, reporting data centre operators shall communicate to the European database the information and key performance indicators set out in Annex I and Annex II regarding the data centre they operate (Art. 3)

Waste heat reused (ERHusr), in kWh shall be measured as defined by, and by using the methodology set out in, the CEN/CENELEC EN 50600-4-6 standard or equivalent. Data centres shall measure the heat that is used or reused outside of the data centre boundary, and which substitutes partly or totally energy needed outside the data centre boundary (Annex II(j))

The information, and key performance indicators, communicated to the European database, and the data centre sustainability indicators, in accordance with Annex III, shall be made public in an aggregated manner, at Member State and Union level (Art. 5(2))

result.title: Regulation and planning of district heating in Denmark
result.summary: This Danish Energy Agency document describes the regulatory framework governing district heating in Denmark, focusing on the Heat Supply Act as the primary law regulating public heating supply installations. It details municipal heat planning obligations, connection mandates (both new and existing buildings), cost-based pricing principles, non-profit operational rules, and approval requirements. The system emphasizes municipal control, cost-reflective tariffs, and integrated heat planning to maximize efficiency and renewable energy integration.

key_articles.requirement: Regulates public heating supply installations including block heating stations with heat output up to 25 MW and CHP units with heating output up to 25 MW

key_articles.ref: Heat Supply Act - Municipal Heat Planning
key_articles.requirement: Municipalities must prepare and update municipal heat plans; the City Council makes final decisions on heating planning and expansion of heat supply; municipalities map existing heat demand, existing supply methods, future demand estimates, and heat supply possibilities

City Council can impose buildings to connect to public heat supply; obligation applies to new buildings and can be imposed on existing buildings after a nine-year grace period following the City Council's decision; connection obligation becomes immediately effective for the City Council decision
Consumers may be exempted from connection obligation or obligation to remain connected for new low-energy buildings or demolition and reconstruction of new low-energy buildings

key_articles.ref: Heat Supply Act - Project proposal requirement
key_articles.requirement: When a DH network is established, changed, or major changes made to existing system (fuel, technical concept, production expansion), a socioeconomic project proposal must be prepared and sent to municipality for approval; must include socioeconomic, user-economic, company-financial, and environmental analyses of different heating supply alternatives

Public heat supply is subject to non-profit rules; supply services must not result in indirect taxation of consumers; municipality not allowed to give subsidies to any users of utility service; DH company itself is subject to non-profit principle

Heating price is set by law to cover all necessary costs related to heating supply; heating supply company not permitted to make profit; only expenses qualifying as 'necessary expenses' can be included in heat price; costs include fuel, heating production facility, DH network, buildings, and operation and maintenance

key_articles.ref: Heat Supply Act - Electricity law exemption
key_articles.requirement: Large CHP plants (producing electricity) are regulated by electricity law; however, heating supply from these plants remains regulated under heat supply law

key_articles.ref: Heat Supply Act - Fuel choice rules
key_articles.requirement: For CHP (cogeneration), more or less all fuel types can be chosen; for heat only boilers without cogeneration, fuel types allowed depend on whether DH facility is in area with or without natural gas supply; areas with natural gas: only natural gas for heat only boilers; areas without natural gas: biomass, waste, biogas, landfill gas, other gasified biomass

key_articles.ref: Heat Supply Act - Ban on electric heating
key_articles.requirement: National ban on electric heating in new buildings introduced in 1993; extended in 1994 to prevent installation of electric heating in existing buildings with water-based central heating systems in areas with DH or gas supply; ban on electric heating still in effect although new low-energy buildings are exempt

compliance_triggers.condition: A building is located in a municipal area where heat supply has been planned and the City Council decides mandatory connection
compliance_triggers.consequence: Building owner is obligated to connect to public district heating network and pay connection fee and/or fixed annual fee to heat supply company; obligation becomes effective immediately upon City Council decision for new buildings; for existing buildings, nine-year grace period applies before mandatory connection can be enforced

compliance_triggers.condition: DH company wishes to establish new DH network, make major change to existing network (fuel type, technical concept, production expansion)
compliance_triggers.consequence: Must prepare socioeconomic project proposal with analysis of heating supply alternatives; proposal must be sent to municipality for approval before project proceeds; proposal must include socioeconomic, user-economic, company-financial, and environmental analyses

compliance_triggers.condition: DH company operates under heat supply law and generates operating costs or revenue
compliance_triggers.consequence: Non-profit principle applies: all costs must be cost-based; no subsidies to any user; company not permitted to make profit; only 'necessary expenses' can be included in heat price; expenses must be justifiable as directly related to heating supply

compliance_triggers.condition: DH company determines heating tariff and pricing structure
compliance_triggers.consequence: Heat price must cover all necessary costs (fuel, production facility, DH network, buildings, operation and maintenance); price is consumer-controlled by cost-based regulation; cost division typically fixed part (connection/capacity) and variable part (per GJ consumption); company cannot pass through expenses unrelated to heating supply

compliance_triggers.condition: DH company seeks to establish or change fuel type for heat production (especially in areas with natural gas supply)
compliance_triggers.consequence: Fuel choice is constrained by regulation: for CHP any fuel type allowed; for heat-only boilers in areas with natural gas supply, only natural gas permitted; for heat-only boilers in areas without natural gas supply, biomass/waste/biogas/landfill gas/gasified biomass allowed; biomass fuel is exempt from taxation

compliance_triggers.condition: Municipality plans municipal heat supply and heating expansion; multiple heating supply options are being considered
compliance_triggers.consequence: Municipality must conduct heat planning using socioeconomic cost-benefit analysis; planning must identify priority heat supply options, locations for future supply units, heat demand projections, and supply possibilities; must map existing supply methods; decision authority is City Council; municipality responsible for ensuring plan alignment with regional and national energy policy goals

compliance_triggers.condition: New building is constructed or building undergoes renovation in area with DH supply available
compliance_triggers.consequence: Building cannot be equipped with electric heating systems (ban on electric heating applies except for new low-energy buildings); if DH is available, building may be required to connect per municipal decision; nine-year grace period exemptions apply in certain renovation scenarios

compliance_triggers.condition: DH company produces electricity through CHP plant (25 MW or less heating output)
compliance_triggers.consequence: Electricity generation regulated under electricity law; heating supply portion regulated under heat supply law; cost allocation between heat and electricity follows statutory rules (typically 120% fiscal heat production efficiency); electricity from biomass CHP receives add-on to market price (EUR 20/MWh or similar renewable subsidy) through 2018; after 2018 only renewable-source CHP receives subsidy

compliance_triggers.condition: DH company seeks to include depreciation, reserves, or return on invested capital in heat price
compliance_triggers.consequence: Depreciation of assets and reserves for future investments allowable as necessary expenses; interest on invested capital may be included in special cases; overall principle is that only expenses directly necessary for heating supply can be included; cross-subsidization with other utility services (e.g., electricity) prohibited to prevent indirect consumer taxation

compliance_triggers.condition: Consumer disputes DH company decision on pricing, service quality, or connection obligation
compliance_triggers.consequence: Private consumer complaints about DH companies handled by Energy Appeal Board within the energy area; appeals of municipal authority decisions can be directed to Energy Appeal Board, Ministry of Energy Utilities and Climate, Danish Energy Regulatory Authority, and individual municipalities; Danish Energy Regulatory Authority handles general tariff and terms issues; Energy Appeal Board handles case-specific disputes

compliance_triggers.condition: DH facility operates in area with both potential CHP and heat-only boiler options
compliance_triggers.consequence: Choice of technology must be based on socioeconomic cost analysis conducted per Danish methodology; City Council approves project proposal based on cost-benefit analysis showing project alternative with largest socioeconomic benefit; cost analysis must use standardized assumptions from Danish Energy Agency (fuel prices, electricity prices, emission costs, technology specifications)

result.temperature_signals: Low-temperature district heating is identified as a key future development. Most current Danish DH networks operate at 80 C supply temperature with 40-45 C return temperature. Modern systems with underfloor heating achieve these return temperatures. Future low-temperature systems are expected to reach 50-25 C flow/return, enabling integration of surplus industrial heat, heat pumps (COP improves with lower delta-T), solar heating (seasonally stored), and geothermal energy. Lower temperatures reduce heat losses in pipelines and increase efficiency of thermal power plants (especially flue gas condensation). Low-temperature DH is noted as particularly relevant for new buildings with modern heating systems but challenging for older buildings with radiator systems requiring higher supply temperatures. The document indicates that lower return temperatures are key to optimizing heat pump efficiency and expanding DH to smaller towns and villages where heating density is lower.
result.transaction_cost_signals: Strong administrative burden and transaction friction are embedded in Danish DH regulation: (1) Municipal heat planning requirement creates recurring planning cycles and multi-stakeholder coordination (municipalities, counties, utilities); (2) Project proposal mechanism requires comprehensive socioeconomic and environmental analysis before approval, using Danish Energy Agency standardized data; (3) Connection obligation imposes municipal authority decisions that trigger potential appeals to Energy Appeal Board, creating dispute resolution overhead; (4) Non-profit principle requires detailed cost accounting and segregation of heating from other utility activities (electricity cross-subsidization prohibited); (5) Cost-based pricing regulation requires transparent cost allocation and consumer-approved tariff structures; (6) Approval of fuel changes, technical modifications, or production expansion requires municipal project review; (7) Socioeconomic analysis methodology (with scrap values, reinvestment costs, externalities) adds analytical complexity. These mechanisms ensure public benefit but impose significant administrative costs on DH operators, municipalities, and consumers.
notable_quotes: The most important law in Danish heating supply is the Heat Supply Act. This act regulates public heating supply installations (including so-called 'block heating stations') with a heat output of more than 250 kW and CHP units with a heating output of up to 25 MW.

The obligation to connect means that the City Council can impose buildings to connect to the public heat supply. This effectively means that the consumers are obligated to pay a connection fee and/or a fixed annual fee to the heat supply company, whether or not they use heating.

The public heat supply is subject to non-profit rules and regulation. The non-profit principle is defined from the following two municipal law principles: Supply services must not result in indirect taxation of the consumers. In other words, the municipality is not allowed to increase its income through utility services.

It is the DH company itself which is subject to the non-profit principle. All services and supplies to the DH company in terms of fuel supply, legal assistance and consulting services are considered commercial activities.

result.title: Excess heat potentials of industrial sites in Europe (sEEnergies WP5 D5.1)
result.summary: This is a technical assessment of excess heat potentials from energy-intensive industries (steel, cement, paper, glass, chemicals, refineries, aluminium) across EU28+. The study analyzes 1608 industrial sites using GIS mapping and process-specific heat calculations across three temperature levels (25°C, 55°C, 95°C) to quantify exploitable waste heat for district heating systems. Total identified potential is 425 PJ at 95°C and 960 PJ at 25°C, with 151 PJ available within 10km of existing/expected district heating areas.

key_articles.topic: Excess heat potential definition and temperature levels
key_articles.requirement: Three reference temperatures define excess heat potentials: Level 1 (25°C) for low-temperature district heating and heat pumps, Level 2 (55°C) for 4th generation district heating, Level 3 (95°C) for conventional 3rd generation district heating systems

425 PJ of excess heat available at 95°C temperature (Level 3), with 960 PJ available at lower 25°C temperature (Level 1), equaling 4% and 9% of total industrial final energy demand in EU28 (2015) respectively

key_articles.topic: Industrial site database and excess heat calculation
key_articles.requirement: 1889 sites with production data and 1653 sites with quantified excess heat potentials identified in EU28; calculation uses formula EH = P × SECProcess × f × 1000 where f is excess heat factor dependent on temperature level and internal heat recovery rate

key_articles.topic: Sectoral excess heat potentials by temperature band
key_articles.requirement: Glass industry recuperative furnaces: 2.6 GJ/tonne (25°C), 1.9 (55°C), 1.8 (95°C); Cement wet kilns: 1.1 (25°C), 0.8 (55°C), 0.7 (95°C); Iron and steel coke ovens: 1.7 (25°C), 1.2 (55°C), 1.1 (95°C); Chemical ethylene production: 6.3 (25°C), 1.8 (55°C), 1.1 (95°C) GJ/tonne

key_articles.topic: District heating area matching and potentials
key_articles.requirement: 12,283 expected district heating areas matched with industrial sites; 1802 sites (98% of 1842 total) have spatial match to expected district heating areas; Selected potential 1 of 1569 PJ at Level 1 (25°C) available within 10km radius of expected DH areas

key_articles.topic: Process-specific exhaust gas temperatures and heat factors
key_articles.requirement: Glass regenerative furnaces: 980°C exhaust, 60% heat loss at 25°C; Cement dry kilns: 450°C exhaust, 20% at 25°C; Steel blast furnaces: 220°C BFG and 250°C blast stove off-gases; BOF: 1700°C with 0.56 GJ/tonne at 25°C (30% diffusion); Pulp/paper boilers: 260°C (no recovery) or 177°C (with recovery), 9% waste at 25°C

key_articles.requirement: Heat demand density classes 3, 4, 5 (≥500 GJ/ha) used to identify expected district heating areas; Class 5 represents very dense urban (≥3000 GJ/ha), Class 4 dense (1200-3000 GJ/ha), Class 3 moderate (500-1200 GJ/ha) concentrations

result.temperature_signals: "The study defines three operational temperature tiers for industrial excess heat: Level 1 (25°C) targets low-temperature district heating and large-scale heat pump applications; Level 2 (55°C) represents 4th generation district heating transition temperature; Level 3 (95°C) corresponds to conventional 3rd generation district heating systems. Glass regenerative furnaces (980°C exhaust) can supply all three levels with heat factors of 60%, 47%, 45% respectively. Steel BOF processes (1700°C) achieve highest waste heat at 25°C (0.56 GJ/tonne) requiring advanced suppressed combustion (70% diffusion). Cement kilns (450°C) yield 1.1-0.7 GJ/tonne across the three levels. Lower-temperature streams (ethylene cracking post-recovery at 150°C, pulp/paper boilers at 177-260°C) concentrate primarily at Level 1 (25°C) potential. This stratification creates a tiered industrial heat supply profile: high-temperature sectors (steel, glass, cement) dominant at all three levels; chemical and refinery sectors shift progressively toward lower-temperature applications with Level 1 contributing 6.3 GJ/tonne (ethylene) vs. 1.1 at Level 3."
result.transaction_cost_signals: The study identifies multiple regulatory and administrative cost drivers affecting industrial excess heat recovery deployment: (1) Database development burden: matching 1889 industrial sites across seven heterogeneous emission/production datasets (E-PRTR, EU ETS, sector-specific databases) required manual validation and coordinate correction; 533 entries (28%) could not be auto-matched and required internet research; (2) Process definition complexity: differing NACE code definitions (4-digit EU standard) vs. ETS activity types create inconsistency in sector classification, requiring manual review of production processes to confirm excess heat eligibility; (3) District heating system verification: only 940 of 12,283 expected district heating areas have confirmed active systems, necessitating field-level validation; (4) Spatial matching friction: 10km search radius for industrial-DH coupling achieved 98% match rate but requires GIS analysis and feasibility engineering for each site; (5) Data quality gatekeeping: 234 industrial sites (13%) lack production data, forcing choice between conservative estimation or exclusion; (6) Certification requirements: diffusion rate assumptions (30-100% internal recovery by sector) require periodic audit and technology tracking to determine what external heat is legally available; (7) No single regulatory framework: analysis spans EU28 + CH, NO, IS with varying heat-to-cooling regulations, energy efficiency directives, and district heating support mechanisms, creating multi-jurisdiction compliance burden for cross-border projects."
notable_quotes: For the 1608 industrial sites in EU28, excess heat potentials ranging between 960 and 190 PJ are identified, depending on the different excess heat utilisation rates. For Level_1 (25°C) at current level of internal heat recovery the highest potential of 960 PJ was determined. When internal heat recovery is reduced it to 692 PJ. If the excess heat is available at the temperature level of 55°C (Level_2), which corresponds to typical temperatures of 4th generation district heating systems, the current available potential amounts to 503 PJ, at full internal recovery reduced to 263 PJ. At temperatures of 95°C (Level_3), the typical conventional district heating system temperatures, a potential of 425 PJ and currently at full internal recovery respectively are identified. (Executive Summary, p. 4)

151 PJ of excess heat could be used within a 10km range at a temperature of 95°C, which is compatible with most existing district heating systems. As district heat today has a total final energy consumption of 1,945 PJ, this means that about 8% of district heating in the EU28 could be supplied by excess heat sources from energy-intensive industries. (Executive Summary, p. 4)
The analysis covers the major industrial excess heat sources (large heavy industry facilities) and the most important excess heat streams: flue gases. (Section 1, p. 13)

Three reference temperatures define excess heat potentials: 25°C to estimate maximum heat attainable if gas is cooled to ambient temperatures (usable with large-scale heat pumps for low-temperature district heating), 55°C for 4th generation district heating grids at lower temperature, and 95°C for typical 3rd generation district heating which corresponds to many systems in place in Europe. (Section 2.2, p. 16)

result.title: Special event: Exploitation of waste heat potentials in Europe
result.summary: This 119-page document is a collection of conference presentations from SDEWES 2017 in Dubrovnik on waste heat exploitation across Central Europe. It consists of the CE-HEAT Interreg project overview, technical case studies on ORC systems and biogas plants, regional waste heat assessments for Croatia, Austria, and Thuringia, and waste heat cadastre development initiatives. The document is purely project-focused and contains no regulatory directives, policy frameworks, or compliance requirements.

result.title: EU Energy Efficiency Directive - Development and Review of Cost Benefit Analysis Exemption Thresholds as required by Article 14(6)
result.summary: This technical document by Ricardo-AEA develops cost-benefit analysis (CBA) exemption thresholds under EED 2012/27/EU Article 14(6) for industrial waste heat recovery and district heating/cooling networks. It establishes distance, minimum heat demand, and minimum available waste heat thresholds to determine when CBA is required; uses discounted cash flow modelling with 20-year investment life and 6% discount rate to identify economic viability breakpoints for heat linking projects using water and steam as transfer media.

result.temperature_signals: The document does not specify temperature bands or process temperature ranges; it treats heat generically in terms of grades (water-based vs. steam-based) and capacity but does not differentiate by supply/process temperature levels (low/medium/high °C) or manufacturing tiers. Water-based heat links are distinct from steam-based links (requiring higher capital costs and shorter viable distances), but no explicit temperature thresholds (e.g., 65°C, 120°C, 160°C) are provided.
result.transaction_cost_signals: CBA requirement itself is the primary regulatory transaction cost lever under Article 14(5)(c/d) — it mandates detailed cost-benefit analysis for large industrial installations and district heating networks. The document proposes exemption thresholds (distance, minimum demand, minimum available heat) to reduce this burden. Member State implementation of thresholds would require: defining capacity-dependent search radius rules (2-15 km for water; 3-15 km for steam); establishing minimum heat demand criteria (100-500 kWth); metering and heat quantification to demonstrate available waste heat; assessment of heat user compatibility (grade matching); and operator burden of demonstrating exemption eligibility. Absence of standardized thresholds forces case-by-case CBA, raising administrative costs and approval friction for heat linking projects.
notable_quotes: Article 14 paragraph 5 of the EED requires that a Cost Benefit Analysis (CBA) be carried out in particular instances occurring after 5th June 2014. Two of the four instances identified are: Article 14(5)(c) [industrial installation with thermal input ≥20 MWth planned or substantially refurbished] and Article 14(5)(d) [district heating/cooling network with thermal input >20 MW(GCV) that is new or substantially refurbished].

Purpose of CBA is to consider the possibility of using waste heat to satisfy economically justified demand, including through cogeneration or connection of the installation to a district heating/cooling network.
Paragraph 6 advises that Member states will be permitted to lay down thresholds...to exempt individual instances listed above from the need to conduct a CBA.

The thresholds values should represent the limit of economic viability under the most favourable conditions. This is to ensure that installations are only exempted from the requirement to perform a cost-benefit analysis where the supply of heat is highly unlikely to be economically viable.
